findings.title: TLS 1.0 is accepted
findings.why: TLS 1.0 has been deprecated by RFC 8996 and is disabled in every current browser. It is vulnerable to BEAST and to downgrade attacks, and it fails PCI DSS.
findings.detail: The server completed a TLS 1.0 handshake.
findings.evidence:
TLS 1.0: accepted (TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA)
TLS 1.1: accepted (TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA)
TLS 1.2: accepted (TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256)
TLS 1.3: accepted (TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256)

findings.title: Plain HTTP is served without redirecting to HTTPS
findings.why: Anything served over HTTP can be read and rewritten in transit. If the same content is reachable over both schemes, an on-path attacker simply keeps the user on the insecure one.
findings.detail: http://example.com returned 200 and ended at http://example.com/ without upgrading to HTTPS.

findings.title: Server accepts cipher suites without forward secrecy
findings.why: Static-RSA key exchange means a single future compromise of the private key decrypts every session ever recorded. ECDHE removes that risk.
findings.detail: 5 accepted suites use static RSA key exchange: TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384.

findings.title: TLS 1.1 is accepted
findings.why: TLS 1.1 is deprecated by RFC 8996 and relies on MD5/SHA-1 in its handshake signatures. No current client needs it.
findings.detail: The server completed a TLS 1.1 handshake.

findings.title: No Strict-Transport-Security header
findings.why: Without HSTS the first request of every session can be downgraded to plain HTTP by an on-path attacker, and the redirect to HTTPS happens too late to protect the cookies already sent.
findings.detail: No Strict-Transport-Security header on the HTTPS response.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy header
findings.why: Without a CSP the browser will execute any script the page references or injects, so any HTML injection becomes script execution. CSP is the only defence-in-depth layer that survives a templating mistake.
findings.detail: No Content-Security-Policy or Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header was returned.

findings.title: CSP restricts nothing for scripts
findings.why: Neither script-src nor default-src is present, so script loading is unrestricted.
findings.detail: No enforced Content-Security-Policy applies, so this control has nothing to restrict it.

findings.title: Certificate expires in less than 30 days
findings.why: Renewal automation fails quietly more often than it fails loudly. Thirty days is the last point at which a failure is still comfortable to fix.
findings.detail: The certificate expires on 2026-10-27T22:17:21Z, in 28 days.

findings.title: No X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
findings.why: Without nosniff, browsers may MIME-sniff a user-uploaded file as HTML or JavaScript and execute it in your origin. It also enables cross-origin script inclusion of JSON endpoints.
findings.detail: No X-Content-Type-Options header, so browsers may MIME-sniff responses whose declared type they distrust.

findings.title: No Referrer-Policy header
findings.why: Browser defaults differ. Where the default is still no-referrer-when-downgrade, the full URL of your page, including any tokens in the path or query, is sent to every third-party host you reference.
findings.detail: No Referrer-Policy header, so the browser default applies and it is not the same in every browser.

findings.title: CSP does not set base-uri
findings.why: base-uri does not fall back to default-src. Without it an injected <base> tag rewrites every relative script URL on the page, which bypasses a host allowlist entirely.
findings.detail: No enforced Content-Security-Policy applies, so this control has nothing to restrict it.

findings.title: CSP has no default-src fallback
findings.why: Fetch directives you did not list fall back to default-src. Without it, connect-src, font-src, frame-src, worker-src and friends are completely unrestricted.
findings.detail: No enforced Content-Security-Policy applies, so this control has nothing to restrict it.

findings.title: CSP does not set frame-ancestors
findings.why: frame-ancestors is the modern clickjacking control and does not fall back to default-src. Without it (and without X-Frame-Options) the page can be framed by anyone.
findings.detail: No enforced Content-Security-Policy applies, so this control has nothing to restrict it.

findings.title: Server accepts CBC-mode cipher suites
findings.why: CBC with MAC-then-encrypt has produced a decade of padding-oracle and timing attacks (Lucky13 and successors). AEAD suites have no equivalent history.
findings.detail: 9 accepted suites use CBC mode: TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256, TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA.

findings.title: No Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header
findings.why: Without COOP a page you open, or that opens you, keeps a window reference across origins. That reference is the basis of tabnabbing and of several XS-Leaks.
findings.detail: No Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header, so cross-origin documents can retain a window reference to this page.

findings.title: No Permissions-Policy header
findings.why: Powerful features stay available to the document and, in some cases, to embedded third-party frames. Denying what you do not use limits what injected or embedded code can reach.
findings.detail: No Permissions-Policy header, so camera, microphone, geolocation and payment keep their default availability.

findings.title: No X-Frame-Options header
findings.why: With neither X-Frame-Options nor CSP frame-ancestors the page can be framed by any site, which enables clickjacking.
findings.detail: Neither X-Frame-Options nor CSP frame-ancestors restricts who may frame this page.

findings.title: CSP does not set object-src 'none'
findings.why: Legacy plugin content (<object>, <embed>) can execute script in some browsers. object-src 'none' is free to deploy and closes that path.
findings.detail: No enforced Content-Security-Policy applies, so this control has nothing to restrict it.

findings.title: CSP restricts nothing for stylesheets
findings.why: Neither style-src nor default-src is present, so stylesheet loading and inline styles are unrestricted.
findings.detail: No enforced Content-Security-Policy applies, so this control has nothing to restrict it.

findings.title: No /.well-known/security.txt
findings.why: Without a published contact, someone who finds a vulnerability has to guess where to send it, and often gives up or goes public instead.
findings.detail: https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt returned 404.

findings.title: Session resumption is not offered
findings.why: Resumption is a latency optimisation. Disabling it is a defensible trade-off in exchange for simpler forward-secrecy reasoning.
findings.detail: A second handshake with the same session cache did not resume.

findings.title: No Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header
findings.why: COEP is only needed if you want crossOriginIsolated (SharedArrayBuffer, precise timers). It breaks third-party embeds that do not opt in, so its absence is reported, not penalised.
findings.detail: No Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header, so the document is not cross-origin isolated.

findings.title: No Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header
findings.why: CORP tells the browser who may embed this response. It is the cheapest mitigation for Spectre-style cross-origin leaks of resource contents.
findings.detail: No Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header, so other origins may embed this response.

findings.title: Server header present without a version
findings.why: The product name alone is low-value information. Suppressing it entirely is cheap but optional.
findings.detail: Server names the product but not a version.
findings.subject: Server

findings.title: Server advertises modern protocols over ALPN
findings.why: ALPN negotiation offers HTTP/2.
findings.detail: ALPN negotiated: h2, http/1.1.

findings.title: Server enforces its own cipher suite order
findings.why: The server, not the client, decides which suite is used.
findings.detail: The server selected the same suite regardless of the order the client offered them.

findings.why: The server provides a fresh revocation proof in the handshake.

findings.title: CORS configuration is sound
findings.why: The server does not expose credentialed responses to arbitrary origins.
findings.detail: No Access-Control-Allow-Origin was returned for a foreign origin.

findings.why: Only safe methods are advertised and TRACE is refused.

findings.title: No plain-HTTP subresource references found
findings.why: The retrieved HTML references no http:// subresources.
findings.detail: No http:// subresource references were found in the retrieved HTML.

findings.title: No version-disclosing headers
